title: Attention-weighted split-merge generation scheduler
creator: Lena Thompson
description:
Problem statement:
Current generation scheduling treats prefill-like (long token prefixes) and short interactive decodes uniformly which causes two recurring issues: (1) long attention-heavy requests can block low-latency interactive decodes, increasing p95/p99 latency for interactive tenants; (2) kernels with very different execution characteristics (dense attention vs. sparsity-optimized kernels, quantized paths) are chosen without considering immediate scheduling impact, leading to suboptimal throughput/latency trade-offs under mixed workloads.

Goal:
Design and implement an adaptive "split-and-merge" generation scheduler that: (a) splits long attention-dense requests into timeboxed sub-phases to improve multiplexing with short decodes; (b) merges small underutilized micro-slices opportunistically to preserve throughput efficiency; (c) factors per-request kernel-selection hints (attention density, kv-cache size, quantization path) into scheduling decisions to reduce stall and kernel-switch overheads; (d) enforces tenant-aware fairness with latency headroom budgets to avoid starvation.

Design highlights (high level):
- Attention-weighted slicing: annotate incoming requests with an attention-density estimator (based on token lengths, model architecture heuristics, and a small prefill probe). Use this score to decide an initial split into micro-phases (timeboxed token windows, e.g., 8–32 token windows) rather than monolithic execution for long jobs.
- Merge policy: maintain a short opportunistic merge window (e.g., 50ms) where adjacent micro-slices with compatible kernel hints and similar latency SLOs are coalesced onto a single kernel run to avoid throughput loss from over-fragmentation.
- Kernel hint propagation: augment request descriptors with kernel affinity hints (dense-attn, sparse-attn, quantized-FP8/INT8) produced by the model-onboarding classifier or runtime probe; scheduler prefers to colocate slices that can use the same execution path to avoid kernel reloads or expensive reconfiguration.
- Tenant fairness and latency headroom: each tenant is assigned a moving headroom budget (ms) derived from recent SLA usage; scheduler uses proportional credits to ensure tenants consuming few tokens but requiring low latency keep priority while high-throughput tenants are rate-limited by soft token quotas during congestion.
- Backpressure and fallback: when merge heuristics or kernel affinity can't be satisfied under high load, the scheduler triggers fallback policies: downgrade to lower-latency kernels (if model fidelity allows), re-prioritize interactive slices, or queue larger jobs to dedicated burst capacity pools.

Metrics and acceptance criteria:
- Latency: p95 interactive decode latency decreases by >=20% in mixed workloads (interactive 30% of requests, long-prefill 70%).
- Throughput: overall token/sec should not drop more than 5% compared to baseline on synthetic throughput workloads after merge tuning.
- Kernel churn: measured kernel-change events per minute should decrease by >=30% relative to naive scheduler under mixed-kernel workloads.
- Fairness: no tenant experiences >2x increase in p95 compared to tenant-specific baseline for more than 5 minutes during sustained load.

Implementation plan:
1) Prototype in runtime scheduler feature-flagged path (runtime/scheduler/aw_splitmerge). Initial prototype uses simple static probe heuristics and in-memory micro-slice queue.
2) Add kernel-hint API in request envelope and extend model onboarding classifier to emit hints.
3) Implement merge heuristics and kernel-coalescing planner.
4) Integrate tenant headroom accounting with existing QoS/credits service.
5) Run cluster-scale simulation using the workload-sim harness and real token traces from past 30 days.
6) Canary on dedicated pool, capture per-tenant telemetry and compare to control.

Open risks and trade-offs:
- Over-splitting increases scheduling overhead and may harm throughput without a strong merge policy. Need careful microbenchmarking of split window sizes and merge latency.
- Kernel affinity estimation errors can cause suboptimal coalescing; mitigate by conservative merge thresholds and fast recovery paths.
- Complexity of tenant-credit interactions may require iterative policy tuning and observability surfaces to debug per-tenant regressions.

- Workload sims: https://internal.redwood.ai/wrk-sim/aw-splitmerge/2026-02-report.pdf

comments: 2026-02-21 — Initial design posted to Confluence; requested feedback from kernel team and platform QoS owners (cc @Arjun Verma, @Maya Chen).
2026-02-28 — Kernel team ran microbenchmarks showing merge-window of 40ms gives best kernel-change vs latency tradeoff on A100; recorded results in sim report.

2026-03-03 — Prototype PR opened (#8392). Early profiler traces show kernel churn down ~22% in small-scale run but p95 regression for tenant T42 in one scenario — investigating tenant headroom tuning.
2026-03-07 — Design review: decided to make attention-density estimator pluggable and default to conservative thresholds; added requirement to surface per-merge decision logs to simplify debugging.
2026-03-10 — Merged prototype behind feature flag to staging dedicated pool; starting canary (10% of traffic) next week. Created follow-up ticket to add adaptive split-size auto-tuner.
